theory.intro: Breaking a whole number into factors lets you regroup a multiplication into easier steps. Keep every factor when you regroup.
facts: Changing the order or grouping of the factors does not change their product: $(3\times4)\times5=3\times(4\times5)$.
Look for factors that pair to make $10$, $100$ or another round number.
steps: Factorise one number to expose a helpful factor.
Re-group so an easy product (like $\times 100$) is formed.

workedExamples.question_text:
Use helpful factors to calculate mentally:
(a) $38\times5$
(b) $68\times25$.

Calculate mentally by regrouping helpful factors:
(a) $72\times125$
(b) $54\times50$.
Factorise both $26$ and $35$ to form a factor of $10$, then calculate $26\times35$.

For $42\times25$:
(a) find two helpful factorisations of $42$ and use one to calculate the product
(b) complete $42\times25=\square\times50$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) $42=21\times2$ and $42=7\times6$.
The first pairs $2$ with $25$ to make $50$; the second pairs $6$ with $25$ to make $150$.
$42\times25$
$=21\times2\times25$
$=21\times50$
$=1050$
(b) Since $2\times25=50$, the remaining factor is $21$.
$\square=21$

workedExamples.question_text:
(a) A student writes $22\times25=11\times2\times25=11\times100$. Identify the error and give the correct product.
(b) Explain why $(3\times8)\times7=3\times(8\times7)$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) $22=11\times2$ is correct, but $2\times25=50$, not $100$.
$22\times25$
$=11\times2\times25$
$=11\times50$
$=550$
(b) Both sides use the same factors in the same order. Only the grouping changes.
Both sides equal $168$.

foundation.question_text: Factorise $24$ to create a factor pair of $2 \times 5$, then calculate $24 \times 5$.
Use a helpful factorisation to calculate $8 \times 125$.

development.question_text: Choose a factorisation of $16$ that makes $75 \times 16$ easy to calculate.
Factorise $22$ to create a multiple of $90$, then calculate $45 \times 22$.
Use a factor pair in $28$ to calculate $28 \times 250$ mentally.

mastery.question_text:
Find two different factorisations that make $24 \times 25$ easier.
Use one to calculate the product.
Complete the equality $36 \times 25=\square \times 100$, then find the product.
Factorise both $18$ and $35$ to form a factor of $10$, then calculate $18 \times 35$.
